summary: Yan Karaoke says it has patched things up with Reynoldstown and still plans to open its 15,000-square-foot karaoke palace inside the historic Atlanta Dairies by the holidays. The Beltline broke ground on its trickiest trail segment yet near Collier Hills, and the Lantern Parade returns to the Southwest Trail on Sept. 19 for the first time since 2024. The Beltline Marketplace more than doubled its small-business class, East Atlanta Kids Club is opening a skateshop in EAV, and Decatur Day honored the Black Beacon Hill community the city bulldozed decades ago. Plus a hard look at Downtown's diversion center and a rainout at the Food & Wine Festival.

topStory.headline: Yan Karaoke Says Reynoldstown Feud Is Settled Ahead of Atlanta Dairies Opening
topStory.summary: The 15,000-square-foot karaoke bar is on track to open inside the historic Atlanta Dairies by the holidays, and its team says early renderings that alarmed neighbors were out of date.
topStory.body:
If you walked past the Atlanta Dairies this summer and wondered what was going on with the renderings everybody was arguing about, here is where things landed. Yan Karaoke still plans to open its flagship in Reynoldstown by this holiday season, and the team says the neighborhood conflict is behind it, per SaportaReport. The pushback was real. The Dairies are a 1930s Streamline Moderne complex listed on the National Register of Historic Places, but that listing carries no actual legal protection. When renderings surfaced showing changes to the facade and darkened street-level windows, preservationists, the Reynoldstown Civic Improvement League, and NPU-N all raised flags. One NPU representative called it "a hostile move that could have been avoided" from an urban design standpoint, since darkened storefronts cut against the Beltline Overlay District rules. Yan's director of operations, Theodore Williams, says the public saw first-stage renderings that never got updated as the design changed. The details he offers: exterior lights are glued on rather than permanently installed, the "marble" columns are not actually marble, only a couple of bolts will go into the structure for the awning, and windows get a 25 percent tint with interior walls behind them.
What's insideDetails
Size15,000 square feet
Private rooms15 soundproofed karaoke suites
AlsoMultiple cocktail bars, a restaurant, VIP areas
Target openingHoliday season 2026
Tinted glass on a Beltline-facing historic building is still going to bug some people, and Williams says the team is open to more conversations. But a big, busy nightlife anchor at the Dairies is a real bet on this corner of the Southeast Trail.
topStory.imageAlt: The historic Atlanta Dairies complex in Reynoldstown along the Beltline

stories.headline: Beltline Breaks Ground on Its Trickiest Trail Yet as Lantern Parade Returns
stories.summary: A one-mile Northwest Trail link near Collier Hills will bridge over Northside Drive and under I-75, and the Lantern Parade comes back to the Southwest Trail on Sept. 19 for the first time since 2024.
stories.body:
Two pieces of Beltline news this week, one for the long game and one for next Saturday night. The trail. City and Beltline leaders held a formal groundbreaking Sept. 10 for Northwest Trail Segment 3B, a winding one-mile stretch that will connect Monday Night Brewing's The Grove area to the finished trails in Collier Hills and around Bobby Jones Golf Course. It ties together Ardmore, Berkeley Park, Brookwood, Collier Hills, and Loring Heights, according to Urbanize Atlanta. This is the one part of the loop with no old rail corridor to convert. "We have to bob and weave through streets over Northside Drive," Atlanta Beltline Inc. CEO Clyde Higgs told SaportaReport. Planners originally floated a crosswalk across Northside, then chose a pedestrian bridge instead. "It blew the budget for sure, but it was the right thing to do for our community," Higgs said. A second bridge will dip under I-75. Once it opens, roughly 17 of the Beltline's 22 miles will be built. The parade. The Atlanta Beltline Lantern Parade is back after skipping 2025.
  • When: Saturday, Sept. 19. Lineup at 7:15 p.m., stepping off at 8 p.m.
  • Where: Starts near Beulah Colbert Park, winds through neighborhood streets, joins the Southwest Trail at Allene Avenue, and heads north to Lee + White in West End
  • New this year: A route almost half a mile longer, more art installations, and pre-parade family programming
Moving the parade to the Westside was a smart call. That stretch of trail deserves the crowd.
stories.imageAlt: Rendering of the Beltline Northwest Trail pedestrian bridge over Northside Drive

stories.headline: Beltline Marketplace Doubles Its Class and Adds a Stop on Irwin Street
stories.summary: The Beltline's small-business incubator picked 13 entrepreneurs from more than 125 applicants and opened a fourth location, Marketplace @ Irwin, on the Eastside Trail in Old Fourth Ward.
stories.body:
Those little shipping-container shops along the trail just got a lot more interesting. The Atlanta Beltline Marketplace, which gives local entrepreneurs cheap commercial space and business mentoring, has grown its new class to 13 businesses, more than double the six in its last round, per Rough Draft Atlanta. Eighty-five percent of the new class is Black-owned, and the group was chosen from more than 125 applications. There is also a brand-new spot, Marketplace @ Irwin at 680 Irwin St. NE in Old Fourth Ward. Here is who is where:
LocationBusinesses
@ Irwin (680 Irwin St. NE, Eastside Trail)ELEVEN17, eLo Vegan Lifestyle, Try Deas and Other Treats, Vine & Olive
@ Freedom Parkway (by the Thomas Taylor skatepark, Eastside Trail)Kronchy, Life Bistro, Mason's Super Dogs
@ Pittsburgh Yards (352 University Ave. SW, Southside Trail)Carrot Dog, Coffyn Pyes, Ideal Barber Group, The Creamy Spot by GOAP
@ Allene (1089 Allene Ave. SW, Southwest Trail)Glaciers Italian Ice, Good As Burgers
The vegan and plant-based lean is strong this round, and Kronchy's Mexican-Colombian tacos and arepas are going straight to the top of my list. Rent is the thing that kills most first-time food and retail businesses in intown Atlanta, so a program that takes that off the table on the busiest trail in the city is worth rooting for.
stories.imageAlt: Ribbon cutting at an Atlanta Beltline Marketplace shipping container shop

stories.headline: East Atlanta Kids Club Is Opening a Skateshop on Flat Shoals
stories.summary: The longtime nonprofit plans East Atlanta Skateshop at 481 Flat Shoals Ave., a youth-built third place selling skate gear and kid-designed merch in the heart of EAV.
stories.body:
East Atlanta Kids Club has been working with Southeast Atlanta kids since 1998. Now it wants to give them a hangout on the main drag. The nonprofit is planning East Atlanta Skateshop at 481 Flat Shoals Ave., Suite A, in East Atlanta Village, according to What Now Atlanta. The shop will sell skate goods and merchandise designed by the club's own young people, and the club is pitching it as a third place for teens, somewhere to be that is not school and not home. The club already runs fitness, experiential learning, and STEAM programs outside the classroom.
"We're building this space with our young people and our neighborhood... neighbors who believe East Atlanta's growth should include meaningful spaces for kids and teens." East Atlanta Kids Club
The project is still in permitting, construction has not started, and there is no opening date yet. But as that stretch of Flat Shoals keeps redeveloping, a storefront built for kids instead of another bar is a nice counterweight.
stories.imageAlt: East Atlanta Kids Club skateshop announcement for Flat Shoals Avenue

stories.headline: Decatur Day Honors Beacon Hill, the Black Community the City Displaced
stories.summary: The 37th annual Decatur Day celebrated Beacon Hill, a thriving Black community founded after the Civil War and cleared by urban renewal in the 1950s and 60s, months after the city created a historic district in its name.
stories.body: Decatur Day has been around for 37 years, but this one carried extra weight. The Sept. 5 gathering on the greenspace at 346 W. Trinity Place in Decatur was dedicated to Beacon Hill, the Black neighborhood that once stood there, according to Decaturish. Beacon Hill, once called "the Bottom," was founded by formerly enslaved people after the Civil War. It grew into the center of Black life in Decatur, with its own schools, churches, and businesses. In the 1950s and 60s, ordinance changes, eminent domain, and urban renewal pushed families out and the neighborhood was torn down. "The Black Beacon Hill community was relocated by force, not by choice," organizer Doris Sims Johnson said. This year the city is doing more than remembering. In April, Decatur designated the area part of the Beacon Hill Historic District. At the event, Mayor Tony Powers read a proclamation, telling alumni, "I want to acknowledge how much you did to open doors that never existed before." Former students of Trinity High, Decatur's historically Black school, shared memories, including Callie Flanigan of the Class of 1963: "We weren't rich ... but we were glad to have what we had." The Beacon Hill Grassroots Coalition frames the preservation work as a form of repair, and it is worth sitting with. A lot of the downtown Decatur people love today exists on land that was taken from these families.
stories.imageAlt: Attendees gather at Decatur Day honoring the Beacon Hill community

stories.headline: Downtown's Diversion Center Is Changing Lives, Just Not Enough of Them Yet
stories.summary: The city's all-hours alternative to jail has handled more than 2,000 diversions since opening in January 2025, far short of the 10,000 to 14,000 visitors a year it was built to serve.
stories.body: The idea behind the Center for Diversion and Services in Downtown is simple. When police encounter someone who is homeless, struggling with addiction, or in a mental health crisis and facing a nonviolent misdemeanor, they bring that person somewhere that offers a shower, a meal, and a caseworker instead of a cell. For some people it works exactly as promised. Atlanta Magazine tells the story of James Jones, who had been homeless for two years when an officer found him sheltering outside the library on Ponce de Leon Avenue the day after Thanksgiving 2025. Instead of arresting him for loitering, the officer offered a ride downtown. A caseworker found Jones a bed in a recovery house, helped him get his birth certificate, and got him on a housing waiting list. He has not slept on the street since. The numbers are the problem. Since opening in January 2025, the center has facilitated a little over 2,000 diversions. It was projected to see 10,000 to 14,000 visitors a year. Atlanta Magazine points to underuse and disagreements over how the center delivers care as the main drags on its results. Anyone who has walked Downtown or Midtown lately knows the need is not the issue. The question is whether the city can get officers, service providers, and the center on the same page before patience with the model runs out.
stories.imageAlt: The Center for Diversion and Services in downtown Atlanta

stories.headline: Rain Washes Out Saturday's Food & Wine Festival Tasting Tent, Sunday Still On
stories.summary: Storms forced the Atlanta Food & Wine Festival to cancel Saturday afternoon's Southern Spread Tasting Tent at The Home Depot Backyard, but the evening events and Sunday's finale are going ahead.
stories.body:
Saturday's storms claimed a big one. The Atlanta Food & Wine Festival called off its Southern Spread x Tasting Tent event on Saturday afternoon because of the weather, according to WSB-TV. "Unfortunately, due to the weather in Atlanta, we have made the difficult decision to cancel today's Southern Spread x Tasting Tent event," organizers said. The tents this year are set up at The Home Depot Backyard next to Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Downtown. If you are holding tickets for anything else, the rest of the weekend is still on:
  • Saturday night: Stacked: The Burger Social and Whiskey & Fire, as scheduled
  • Sunday: Homecoming x Tasting Tent, with organizers promising "beautiful weather tomorrow"
A four-day festival losing its Saturday afternoon tent is a tough break for the chefs who prepped all week. Sunday looks like the day to go.
stories.imageAlt: Atlanta Food & Wine Festival tasting tent area
